# Do Not Forget My Teaching: Developing a Biblical-Based Spiritual Pedagogy

Proverbs 1-9 is a highly nuanced foray into a spiritual pedagogy: a study of how people grow in the faith. Fathers and mothers, pastors and counselors, teachers and leaders are given the weighty duty of helping people to make progress in the faith. This means that those who serve in a leadership capacity must become students of human nature. Keen insight into the nature of humanity enhances our ability to be constructive overseers in another's shepherding care. In short, the more we understand how humans work the better we get guiding people in faith development and moral formation.

Strewn throughout Proverbs 1-9 are identifiable elements that contribute to a biblical anthropology: a theological understanding of the essential makeup of humanity. In this opening section of Proverbs, Solomon's lectures to his son help all its readers consider the various aspects of human composition. Humans are complex creatures made up of a multitude of faculties. Typically, people identify the physical (body/material) and spiritual (non-material) dimensions of humanity. Others understand the domains of character, knowledge, and skill. Proverbs offers a unique and nuanced take on human makeup. Understanding Proverbs depiction of human nature—the various faculties of human composition—helps us to focus our learning in transformative ways.

To understand biblical spirituality and to shepherd Christian formation, we must attend to the whole of the human—body (3:8; 4:22; 5:11) and soul (2:10; 3:22). Solomon's lectures address various components of humanity. While we cannot do an exhaustive treatment of this study, we can highlight several components to showcase Proverbs advanced and nuanced anthropology. Solomon addresses human knowledge: what we comprehend and understand (1:2, 4, 7, 29; 2:2-3, 5-6, 9-10; 3:13; 5:1-2; 8:9-10, 12; cf. 9:13). He appeals to affections: the things we love and hate, care for and despise (1:7, 22, 29-30; 3:11; 4:6; 5:12, 19; 6:16, 30; 7:18; 8:13, 17, 21, 36; 9:8). Solomon is concerned about good desires: the things which bring us pleasure, satisfaction, and delight (1:13, 19; 26, 31; 2:10, 14; 3:10, 15, 31; 4:17; 5:18-19; 6:30; 7:18; 8:11, 21, 30-31; 9:17). He is urgent about healthy relationships: the people we attach ourselves to, the associations we make, the intimate relationships we enjoy, and the commitments we establish (1:11, 14-15; 2:17, 19; 4:15; 5:8, 15-20; 6:1, 14, 19). Solomon connects moral formation in wisdom to how one responds to authority: receptivity to God's word, acceptance of God's truth, and submission to God's authority (1:3; 2:1; 3:11; 4:10).

Solomon issues warnings about our conduct: the way we act, behave, and live our lives (1:11, 16; 3:22; 6:18). Proverbs summons us to moral character: a quality of life expressed in virtue, godliness, and righteousness (1:3; 2:7-9, 21; 3:32; 4:11). Along with Solomon's son, we are encouraged to establish and cultivate spirituality: a genuine relationship with the one and only living God based upon faith, trust, and the fear of the Lord. We are enjoyed to develop attention: focus, intentionality, and concentration on what is most important (1:8, 25, 33; 2:2; 3:21; 4:1, 10, 20-21, 23; 4:25; 5:1, 11; 7:24; 8:6, 33-34). Humans must grow in godly attractions: draw toward that which is honorable, noble, and dignified (1:9-10; 3:16, 22, 35; 4:8-9; 5:9; 6:24, 33; 8:6, 15-16, 18; 9:13). Proverbs seeks to train us in correct values: treasuring, keeping, and guarding that which is most precious and important (2:1, 20; 3:1, 3, 9, 14-16; 3:21; 4:4, 8, 13; 5:2; 6:20; 7:1-3; 8:10-11, 19). We are called to train our will: learn to make right decisions and orient our lives on a good trajectory that leads to life and reward (1:10, 23-25, 29, 32; 3:27, 31; 4:26-27; 5:7; 7:25). In addition, we notice the importance of memory (2:17; 3:1; 4:5), speech (2:3; 3:28; 4:24; 5:2; 6:2-3, 17, 19; 8:6-9; 9:12; cf. 2:12, 16; 3:33; 5:3; 6:12, 24; 7:5, 21), emotions (2:14; 3:24-25; 5:18; 8:30-31), loyalty (1:8; 4:2, 4-6; 6:20), inclination (1:28; 2:2-4; 4:20; 5:1, 13), intentions (1:31-32; 2:15, 22; 3:29, 32; 6:13-14, 18), wonder and imagination (8:1-36).

Proverbs 1-9 presents this holistic view of humanity and calls us to specific learning objectives. Whether pastor, parent, or pedagogue, faith leaders should target the following domains and goals: establish true belief (knowledge), develop competency (skill), order loves (affection), shape appetites (desires), stir/reenchant wonder (awe), capture imagination, shape character (virtue), form healthy attachments (relationships), fortify attention, form habits, hone skills, purify motives, reform conduct, and mature attractions. Overarching these domains of learning is a goal to cultivate the fear of God in order to build a biblical worldview.

In the course of these discourses, Solomon also identifies various approaches to formation, helping us develop a distinctively biblical pedagogy to our work in faith formation. Proverbs commends an approach to formation that involves embodied learning, experiential instruction that engages the whole person (4:20-27) and is participatory (2:1-4). It emphasizes the irreplaceability of internalization (interiorization), seeking of for truth to become possessed in the inner being (2:1-4). It highlights the importance of formation in a family (1:8-10, 15; 2:1; 3:1, 11, 21; 4:1, 10-11, 20; 5:1; 6:1, 20; 7:1) and community context (5:14) that is intergenerational (4:1-9). The Scripture already understood what is highly regarded as quality pedagogy today: the importance of modeling, apprenticeship, and experiential learning. When wisdom in the fear of God is understood as the overarching goal of formation, teachers allow for learners to experience appropriate exposure and discovery to the world so that they can one day become full-fledged citizens therein. Within this context, we even see various teaching methods employed and endorsed: lecture, discussion, role playing.

## Key Ideas

- Proverbs offers a spiritual pedagogy—a foundation and framework to understand how people change and grow in the faith.
- Proverbs presents a holistic theological anthropology; Solomon address a variety of domains and faculties that makeup human nature.
- We should embrace proven strategies, approaches, and methods for formation that seek for transformation and change.

## Reflection Questions

<Question id="Pro-Ses6-RefQue-1">1. Who are some of the best teachers you ever had? What made them such impactful teachers?</Question>
<Question id="Pro-Ses6-RefQue-2">2. How does Proverbs 1-9 serve as a spiritual pedagogy: an introduction into formation and transformative learning?</Question>
<Question id="Pro-Ses6-RefQue-3">3. How do these principle help you develop your own skills in parenting, teaching, and ministry?</Question>
